newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Algerian economic blueprint sets ambitious targets.
newsitem.headline: Algerian economic blueprint sets ambitious targets.

text.p: Algeria has sketched an ambitious blueprint for economic growth whose targets will be hard to achieve and depend partly on ending bloodshed, economic analysts said on Sunday.

Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia said on Saturday that the government in the next three years planned to create 1.2 million jobs, build 800,000 homes and lift annual Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth by seven percent from the average four percent.
"The government is serious about trying to meet housing demand and implement a programme on unemployment, but I don't think it can realistically reach those targets," one Western analyst said.

Ouyahia admitted the housing sector faced huge problems, that unemployment had been allowed to grow over years and that ordinary Algerians were probably not yet feeling the benefits of economic development such as lower inflation and higher foreign reserves.

But economic reforms of the past three years were now bringing results and planned financial changes, privatisation, special housing and major works programmes financed by the state, were all causes for "legitimate optimism", he said.

The government was also pursuing exploration and exploitation of the oil and gas on which Algeria relies for over 90 percent of foreign income and which Ouyahia forecast would be earning $15 billion in the year 2000, plus $2 billion in non-energy exports.

"The energy expectations are credible. A lot of money is going into exploration and exploitation. But I don't think they can reach the housing target -- I can't see more than 150,000 units coming on the market each year," said another analyst.
Algerian officials put the housing shortage at one million units, and unemployment at 28 percent, or 2.2 million people.

Overcrowding, lack of hope for a job or home for many young people, who make up more than two-thirds of the 29 million population, are seen as important factors in discontent which fuelled Moslem fundamentalist unrest early in 1992. About 60,000 people have died in the violence which continues.
In the parliamentary debate on the programme on Sunday, the opposition Socialist Forces Front (FFS) accused Ouyahia of producing an ideological discourse instead of a programme.
"We see few figures which give no direction to implement a programme," said Ali Rachedi, an FFS deputy.

Echoing this as far as the construction industry was concerned, one analyst said: "The building sector is in dire straits. People have not been paid for months. A lot of construction is at a standstill."
Special programmes on renewing road and rail infrastructures, which would be labour intensive and soak up some unemployment, would need improved security outside the cities, said the first analyst.
"Much of that sort of work is constrained by (the lack of) security in much of the country," he said, referring to the killings which have particularly hit isolated communities.

The International Monetary Fund, which has a $1.6 billion three-year loan programme for Algeria, also believes insecurity must be resolved if privatisation and investment, important planks in the government programme, are to succeed.

"Establishing a dynamic and growing private sector (is) crucial to reducing unemployment and ensuring sustainable growth...Establishing security and political stability would be an essential precondition for the foreign investment and technology transfers needed for the private sector," it said in July.

Algeria's two-year-old programme of privatisation has signally failed to take off. Many see the policy as at best lukewarm, with officials fearing that huge layoffs would follow any sale of mostly overmanned state firms. A senior official said in July the government planned to sell off 200 to 230 state firms.
One Western analyst said Algeria had rightly focused on macroeconomic reform over the past three years.
This had made manageable the repayment ratio on Algeria's estimated $32 billion foreign debt, cut inflation, and taken foreign reserves to a healthy $6.4 billion credit this month.

"The government knows it has now got to get down to some microeconomic reforms. But I think one of the main obstacles is psychological -- the problem of changing habits from decades of socialist thinking," said an analyst.

"There is still opposition. Sixty percent of GNP is produced today by the public sector. It may come down to 50 percent by the year 2001 but that is still very large state involvement in production of goods and services."
